clue.text: Home team primarily cry — Moore and Hunt wave …

indicators.note: to wave is to move to and fro, so the letters gathered before it are set in motion and rearranged
primarily means firstly, so only the opening letter of team is used

parts.note: taken as written
Bobby Moore, England's 1966 captain, taken as written
Roger Hunt, England forward in 1966, taken as written

explanation.surface: England's home side opens with a roar as Moore and Hunt wave to the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wave' shuffles T (first letter of 'team'), CRY, MOORE and HUNT together. The whole puzzle celebrates England's 1966 World Cup team.
explanation.definitionFit: One's native land is one's home, the nation one belongs to by birth.

clue.text: They draw match, briefly reflecting on scores

indicators.note: a reflection shows things the wrong way round, so the shortened word is turned backwards
briefly says the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a match is a game
a striker who scores nets the ball

explanation.surface: A drawn match, summed up briefly while reflecting on the scores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the last letter and 'reflecting' turns the rest round; in a down clue 'on' puts it above the scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnetic bars attract iron, so they draw metal towards them.

clue.text: Stretch and tip over goal, Banks to save

indicators.note: to tip something over is to upend it, so the word for goal is turned around

parts.note: the goal is the net

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so only the outer letters of save are used

explanation.surface: Gordon Banks stretches to tip the ball over the bar and make a save.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip over' turns NET into TEN; 'Banks' gives the edges of 'save', S and E. Gordon Banks was England's 1966 goalkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to make something taut is to pull or strain it tight.

clue.text: Minutes in match that's run over?

definitions.text: Minutes in match that's run over?

indicators.note: in a down entry, over means placed above the rest

parts.note: in cricket an extra is a run not scored off the bat

indicators.note: in puts the letter for minutes inside the word for match

parts.note: a cup match is a tie

explanation.surface: Added minutes are played when a match has run over its normal length.
explanation.walkthrough: M (minutes) goes 'in' TIE to make TIME, with EXTRA (a cricket run) placed 'over' it. The whole clue also defines: 1966's final went to added time.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra minutes added to a drawn knockout match are a period when play runs beyond its normal length.

clue.text: Cohen and Stiles left to dance: do they have shirts on?

indicators.note: letters made to dance jig about into a new order

parts.note: George Cohen, England's 1966 right-back, taken as written
Nobby Stiles, England's 1966 midfielder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Two 1966 players leave the pitch to dance, prompting the question of whether they kept their shirts on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to dance' rearranges COHEN, STILES and L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: Washing is pegged on outdoor drying cords, so shirts hang on them: a playful definition.

clue.text: See 18
Ancient characters try to get up — hard in the morning

indicators.note: in a down entry, getting up means reading from bottom to top, so the word is reversed

parts.note: to have a try is to have a go
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
AM stands for ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: Someone tries to rise early, finding it hard in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get up' turns GO upwards to OG.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an early Irish alphabet carved as notches on standing stones, so its letters are ancient.

clue.text: Moment of courage: overcome

parts.note: to have heart is to have courage
to beat a rival is to overcome them

explanation.surface: A moment of bravery wins the day.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: something done in a single pulse of the pulse takes an instant.

clue.text: Nurse to help, not when time's short

indicators.note: not says the word for when is taken away from the word for help

parts.note: to assist is to help
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: short says the word for time loses its last letter

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A nurse is asked to help, though not when time is short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes AS from ASSIST, leaving SIST; 'short' cuts ERA to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: In British hospitals a senior nurse in charge of a ward holds this title.

clue.text: Stand and drink around student hour

indicators.note: around says the word for drink wraps round the letter for student

parts.note: a pint is a drink of beer
L is for learner, the student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A student stands a round of drinks for an hour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts L inside PINT.
explanation.definitionFit: The base on which a statue or column rests is a pedestal that supports it.

clue.text: Ball part of this? German with English, new World Cup winners?

parts.note: Italy, Italia in Italian, won the World Cup in 1934, 1938 and 1982

explanation.surface: A query about the ball, then Germany, England and Italy listed as World Cup winners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball' is not the football: a ball here is a testicle, which is a part of the reproductive organs.
explanation.definitionFit: Testicles, colloquially balls, are among the external sex organs, so a ball is one part of them.

clue.text: Captains make call in decider?

definitions.meaning: chiefs or leaders, as of a team or department
the call a captain makes when a coin is tossed to decide who kicks off

explanation.surface: The captains each make their call at the coin toss before the match.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaders are the chiefs of groups, and one face of a coin is called at a toss.

clue.text: Some open email offering treatment

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An email that offers some kind of medical treatment, best left unopened.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectal injection of fluid is a medical procedure given to a patient as a remedy.

clue.text: A unit of 11 torn to pieces?

indicators.note: something torn to pieces is broken up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the cross-reference brings in the solution to 11, which is ENEMA
taken as written

explanation.surface: A single item from clue 11 gets ripped apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pieces' rearranges ENEMA (the answer to 11) with TORN.
explanation.definitionFit: A billionth of a metre is a metric measurement of length.

clue.text: Leisurely Wilson's back goes running: that's enough!

indicators.note: running suggests the letters are in motion and mixed up
the back or final letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: Ray Wilson, England's 1966 left-back
sh! is the call for quiet, meaning that's enough

explanation.surface: Ray Wilson is caught running back while someone shouts at him to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back goes' drops the final letter of the 1966 left-back's surname before 'running' shuffles what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unhurried is rather lacking in pace, so a relaxed gait is fairly slow.

clue.text: Desperate as each German chases balls

indicators.note: to chase is to follow, so these pieces come after the word for balls

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls

explanation.surface: A German player chases every ball, desperate to win.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket six balls make an over; 'chases' means follows, so the other pieces come after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone too keen or impatient is desperate to get going.

clue.text: Ties lost (international matches)

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lost, as in league tables
the Ashes is the cricket series between England and Australia

explanation.surface: A record of draws and defeats in matches between nations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ties' looks like drawn games but means binds. The Ashes is the England–Australia Test cricket series.
explanation.definitionFit: To bind something with rope is to fasten or secure it tightly.

clue.text: Protection for players in sack — pulls out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Players' protective gear in a bag gets pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SACK and PULLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Close-fitting caps were worn by cricketers and others as head guards before helmets.

clue.text: Right note sent back for recording device

indicators.note: sending something back returns it, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: a breve is a long musical note

explanation.surface: A right note returned to a recording machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns BREVE to EVERB.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo effect unit used in studios adds resonance to recorded sound.

clue.text: Main feature of 24 — Charlton brothers initially playing

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are in play and moving about, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the cross-reference brings in the solution to 24, which is LINES
Jack and Bobby Charlton both played for England in 1966; the surname is taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter of brothers is used

explanation.surface: The Charlton brothers are the standout figures of the line-up, both playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges LINES (the answer to 24), CHARLTON and B (first letter of 'brothers'). 'Main' is the old poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is the sea, and this broad inlet between Wales and south-west England is a feature of it.

clue.text: See 1
Endlessly support, watch and smile!

indicators.note: endlessly means each of the two words loses its last letter

parts.note: to cheer on a team is to support it
to see is to watch

explanation.surface: A fan cheers, watches and grins as the team plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' cuts CHEER to CHEE and SEE to SE.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers tell people to say this word so their mouths form a grin.

clue.text: Sure a virus enters Jewish school

indicators.note: enters says the virus goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: yes means sure as a reply
HIV is the virus that causes AIDS

explanation.surface: A virus is certain to spread through a Jewish school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enters' places the virus between the word for sure and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An Orthodox academy for studying the Talmud is a religious college for Jews.

clue.text: One strips off, runs back out

parts.note: A means one, as in 'a dog'

indicators.note: running back means going in reverse, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to peel something is to strip off its skin

explanation.surface: A streaker strips off, runs back onto the pitch, and gets sent off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs back' turns PEELS to SLEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sound asleep is out cold, dead to the world.

clue.text: Drunk's personality wanting spirit — time before turning bad?

indicators.note: a drunk slurs the word, turning its S sound into SH

parts.note: one's self is one's personality
life is spirit or liveliness

explanation.surface: A drunkard's character lacks spirit, and there is not long before he turns nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: A slurring drunk says SELF as SHELF. 'wanting' here means needing, a link to LIFE.
explanation.definitionFit: The period a product can be stored before it goes off is its storage duration.

clue.text: Peters and football people leave half cut

parts.note: FA is the Football Association, football's governing body in England

indicators.note: half cut means the word loses half its letters

parts.note: to desert is to leave

explanation.surface: Martin Peters and the football officials leave, half drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half cut' (also British slang for drunk) trims DESERT to DES. Martin Peters scored in the 1966 final.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that peters out gradually dwindles, so the verb means gradually dies away.

clue.text: See 4
No 2 to No 8 cry coming from field?

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for number, as No is

indicators.note: the first No means without, so the letter for two is dropped

parts.note: eight written out
T is the initial letter of two

explanation.surface: Shirt numbers 2 and 8 shout across the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'No T, to N EIGHT': N plus EIGHT with no T. Cohen wore 2 and Hunt 8 in 1966; the field is a horse's meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse in a paddock makes a whinnying noise, its characteristic call.

clue.text: Crowd missing start, Germany moved slowly

indicators.note: the word loses its first letter

parts.note: to wedge people in is to crowd them together
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A crowd that missed kick-off watches Germany creep forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing start' turns WEDGE into EDGE, followed by D.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch carefully forward is to creep along little by little.

clue.text: Fantastic Hurst ultimately is an icon; he led players

indicators.note: ultimately means finally, so the last letter of the name is used
fantastic suggests something fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Geoff Hurst, hat-trick hero of 1966, is a fantastic icon who led his team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' rearranges T (end of 'Hurst') with IS AN ICON. 'Players' are musicians, not footballers.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was a famous Italian conductor who directed orchestras of musicians.

clue.text: Study country and its continent with lecturer

parts.note: Peru is a country in South America
SA is South America, the continent containing Peru

explanation.surface: A lecturer studies a nation and the continent around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A careful read-through of a document is an examination of it.

clue.text: Ask the man, Ken, to drop pants with this problem?

indicators.note: dropping says the letters of the name are removed from the phrase

parts.note: the name's three letters are taken out in order

explanation.surface: Ask a man called Ken to take his trousers down because of his medical issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like trousers, but here it means breathes hard. 'to drop' removes K, E and N from ASKTHEMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheezing chest condition makes sufferers gasp for breath.
